title: Where things are
intro: This unit says where people and things are. It brings the first case ending, the locative `-dA` (in, at, on), the words *bar* and *ýok* for **there is** and **there isn't**, the way endings go onto names, and the words for here and there.

blocks.text: Turkmen has no separate words for **in**, **at** or **on**. An ending on the noun does their job: *öý* (house) becomes *öýde* (at home, in the house), *mekdep* becomes *mekdepde* (at school, in the school), *stol* becomes *stolda* (on the table). Grammars call this ending the locative.

It has two forms, chosen by vowel harmony as in [A1 unit 2](a1-u02): *-da* after a back vowel, *-de* after a front one. The *d* never changes, whatever sound the word ends with, and the last consonant of the word stays as it is: *mekdepde*, *Aşgabatda*.

blocks.label: The locative
lines: -dA  →  -de   after e, ä, i, ö, ü

blocks.text: **With to be.** A place works like the descriptions of [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): put the subject and the place side by side, with no word for **is**. To ask where, use *nirede*, **where**: *Sen nirede?* Where are you? *Öýde.* At home.

items.en: The book is on the table.
Where are you? — In the kitchen.

blocks.text: The negative and the question work as in [A1 unit 4](a1-u04): *däl* after the place, `-mY` onto it.

items.tk: Ýok, ol öýde däl, ol mekdepde.
items.seg: Ýok, ol öý|de däl, ol mekdep|de.
items.en: No, she isn't at home, she's at school.

blocks.title: Where, not where to
blocks.text: The locative says where something **is**, not where it is going. *Men mekdepde* is **I'm at school**. Going **to** school takes another ending, in [A1 unit 7](a1-u07).

sections.title: There is, there isn't: bar and ýok

blocks.text: *bar* says that something **exists** or **is there**; *ýok* says that it **isn't**. They go at the end of the sentence, usually after a place in the locative: *Otagda stol bar.* There is a table in the room. *Otagda oturgyç ýok.* There is no chair in the room.

items.en: There is a market in the city.
There is no water in the kitchen.
Is there a library in the school?

blocks.text: Questions take `-mY` as usual: *barmy?* (is there?), *ýokmy?* (isn't there?). The short answer repeats the word: *Kafe barmy? — Hawa, bar.* Or just *Ýok.*

lines.en: Excuse me, is there a café here?

blocks.text: **köp, many.** To say there are **many** or **a lot**, end with *köp* instead of *bar*: *Aşgabatda dükan köp.* There are many shops in Ashgabat. After *köp* the noun usually stays singular.
**Nobody, nothing.** With *ýok*, *hiç kim* means **nobody** and *hiç zat* means **nothing**: *Öýde hiç kim ýok.* There's nobody at home. *Otagda hiç zat ýok.* There's nothing in the room.

**Someone who isn't there.** With a person, *ýok* says that they are away: *Merdan işhanada ýok*, Merdan isn't at the office. *Merdan işhanada däl* says the same while you point to where he is instead: *işhanada däl, öýde*.

blocks.title: ýok or däl
blocks.text: *ýok* says something **isn't there**; *däl* says what something **is not**. *Bu ýerde kitap ýok*: there is no book here. *Bu kitap däl*: this is not a book.

Names of people, towns and countries keep their capital letter, and endings are written straight onto them, with no apostrophe and no space: *Aşgabatda* (in Ashgabat), *Türkmenistanda* (in Turkmenistan), *Londonda* (in London). The ending follows the last vowel of the name, like any other word.

items.en: Merdan is in London, not in Mary.

blocks.text: As the last example shows, the locative on a person says who **has** something with them: *Kitap Aýnada*, the book is with Aýna.
**Numbers** written in figures take a hyphen before an ending: *2026-njy ýylda*, in (the year) 2026. The numbers come in [A1 unit 11](a1-u11); for now, just notice the hyphen.

blocks.title: No apostrophe
blocks.text: Turkmen never writes an apostrophe before an ending, not even on a name: *Aşgabatda*, *Aýnada*. In this course an answer with an apostrophe is marked **almost**.
*ýer* means **place**, and with *bu*, *şu* and *ol* in the locative it gives the words for **here** and **there**. They are written as two words.

**mende, sende, onda.** The pronouns take the locative too. With *bar* and *ýok* they say what someone has **with them** or **on them**: *Mende pul ýok*, I have no money on me. *Sende ruçka barmy?* Do you have a pen?

head: Pronoun
+ locative
Meaning
rows: on you, with you (plural or polite)

items.en: I have no money on me.
He has a book with him.

blocks.title: onda, with an n
blocks.text: *ol* takes an extra *n* before the ending: *onda*, never *olda*. You will see this *n* again with other endings of *ol*.

blocks.title: Have
blocks.text: *Mende … bar* is about what you have with you or at hand. Saying what you own, such as **my house** or **I have a brother**, uses another pattern, in [A1 unit 9](a1-u09).

summary: The locative `-dA` means in, at or on: *-da* after back vowels, *-de* after front ones, always with *d*: *öýde*, *mekdepde*, *otagda*.
A place works like a description: *Men öýde*; *Öýde däl*; *Öýdemi?* Ask with *nirede*: *Sen nirede?*
*bar* (there is) and *ýok* (there isn't) end the sentence: *Otagda stol bar*. *köp* says there are many.
*hiç kim ýok*: nobody; *hiç zat ýok*: nothing. With a person, *ýok* says they are away.
Names take endings with no apostrophe: *Aşgabatda*, *Aýnada*. Numbers take a hyphen: *2026-njy ýylda*.
*bu ýerde, şu ýerde, ol ýerde*: here, right here, there. *mende, sende, onda* + *bar* or *ýok*: what someone has with them.
